subject: moskovitz

brief.inclusion: Facebook and Asana co-founder whose Democratic giving and Good Ventures-funded philanthropy link technology wealth to elections, global health, science and catastrophic-risk policy.
brief.namesakes: Matched through Dustin A. Moskovitz, Asana/Good Ventures affiliations and San Francisco addresses.

openQuestions: The division of grantmaking authority among Moskovitz, Cari Tuna, Good Ventures and Coefficient Giving varies by program.
Meta-share sales and donations change estimates of personal net worth quickly.

summary: Dustin Moskovitz co-founded Facebook and Asana, then committed with his wife Cari Tuna to give away most of their wealth through Good Ventures and the organization now called Coefficient Giving. Their philanthropy applies effective-altruist methods to global health, science, farm-animal welfare and catastrophic risks, while Moskovitz separately became one of the largest Democratic donors in the 2016, 2020 and 2024 elections.

Good Ventures selects causes using importance, neglectedness and tractability rather than personal familiarity alone.

chapters.title: From Florida to Harvard
chapters.dek: Moskovitz entered technology through a college social network rather than a conventional engineering career.
chapters.body: Born in Florida in 1984, Moskovitz studied economics at Harvard and shared a dormitory with Mark Zuckerberg. He left before graduating as Facebook moved to California, becoming one of the youngest people to acquire a large public-company fortune. [[britannica-facebook, asana-bio, forbes-moskovitz]]

chapters.title: Engineering Facebook's early scale
chapters.dek: Operational responsibility for a fast-growing network created both Moskovitz's wealth and his first experience with large systems.
chapters.body: As co-founder, first chief technology officer and vice president of engineering, Moskovitz helped move Facebook from campuses to a broad social platform. He left in 2008 but retained equity that remained the principal source of his wealth as Facebook became Meta. [[asana-bio, facebook-history, forbes-moskovitz]]

chapters.title: Building tools for coordinated work
chapters.dek: Asana translated lessons about organizational friction into a second software company.
chapters.body: Moskovitz and Justin Rosenstein founded Asana in 2008 to make responsibilities and workflows visible without relying on email. Moskovitz served as CEO through 2025 and chair through 2026, financing the company heavily and retaining a substantial stake through its public listing. [[asana-founders, asana-bio, asana-10k]]

chapters.title: A commitment to give away most wealth
chapters.dek: Good Ventures separated household wealth from a deliberate, long-horizon grantmaking program.
chapters.body: Moskovitz and Cari Tuna created Good Ventures in 2011 after deciding to give away the vast majority of their wealth. Tuna led much of the research and grantmaking design; their account emphasizes moral concern for people and animals regardless of geography or personal connection. [[good-ventures-story, good-ventures-home, pledge]]

chapters.title: From charity evaluation to cause selection
chapters.dek: The partnership with GiveWell expanded from ranking charities to comparing entire fields of action.
chapters.body: Good Ventures partnered with GiveWell in 2012. The resulting Open Philanthropy Project, now Coefficient Giving, evaluates importance, neglectedness and tractability across global health, science, biosecurity, AI risk, criminal justice and animal welfare. The method aims to direct marginal dollars where research predicts the greatest effect. [[givewell-partnership, coefficient-about, coefficient-causes]]

chapters.title: Philanthropy that reaches policy
chapters.dek: Research grants and ballot-measure funding blur no legal categories, but they do share a theory of leverage.
chapters.body: The network funds scientific research and service delivery, but it also supports advocacy and state policy campaigns where legal change may have large effects. Criminal-justice and housing ballot initiatives demonstrated how evidence-driven philanthropy can become a form of political power outside candidate elections. [[axios-ballots, coefficient-causes]]

chapters.title: Exceptional giving against Trump
chapters.dek: Moskovitz describes partisan spending as a response to extraordinary democratic risk rather than his philanthropic default.
chapters.body: In 2016 Moskovitz publicly committed millions to oppose Donald Trump. He expanded that spending in 2020 and gave $50 million to FF PAC in 2024, making him one of the cycle's largest Democratic donors. These are personal political contributions distinct from Good Ventures grants, even when both reflect concern about institutions and long-term risk. [[moskovitz-2016, fec-moskovitz, opensecrets-2024]]

chapters.title: From operating executive to allocator
chapters.dek: Leaving Asana management concentrates attention on board work, ownership, philanthropy and political capital.
chapters.body: Moskovitz stepped down as Asana CEO in 2025 and as chair in 2026 while remaining a board member and adviser. The transition makes the architecture of his influence clearer: public-company stakes supply capital, Good Ventures supplies philanthropic capacity, Coefficient Giving supplies research and recommendations, and personal contributions operate in elections. [[asana-succession, asana-bio, good-ventures-home, fec-moskovitz]]
